Overlappers refuse to end one relationship until they have another one in progress. Oh, please, I corrected her. Of course they do. Even when she pretty much hated the one she was with, she stuck it out until she'd lined up his replacement. I could never understand why. I know -- and have unfortunately dated -- plenty of men who careen from one girlfriend directly into another, often with a big fat overlap; connecting the two relationships like a murky Venn diagram. But however you word it, Overlappers deceive one or both parties in order to get what they want. When you begin a relationship dishonestly, it usually comes back to bite you in the butt. At the very least, you will never be fully able to trust an Overlapper. Because -- as yet another cliche based in truth goes -- if he does it with you, he'll do it to you. 2. Drama! Breakups are never fun, however splits caused by infidelity are hands down the most explosive. If you're like my friend and her man (who, against all odds, actually left his wife), this means that instead of talking about hearts, flowers, and butterflies -- like other new couples -- you spend your nights plotting how to hide assets and whether or not your overpaid lawyer is enough of a shark. How romantic! 3. The Pressure! Though they may appear independent, people who can't be alone are that way because they need to see themselves reflected in someone else's adoring eyes. But when their mirror (aka, partner) develops a flaw (weight gain, job loss, etc.), their image of themselves reflects that. Being a narcissist, nothing less than perfection is acceptable, so they start looking for the next mirror. Got that, fatty? You'd better stay at the top of your game if you want to hang onto an Overlapper. 4. Not cute! "I met my boyfriend when his puppy peed on my foot" is the perfect example of a meet-cute story. It has all the key elements -- chance, humor, and, best of all, a cuddly puppy! "I met my boyfriend because I was his kids' nanny and then his wife found out, which is how I got this black eye," is definitely not a tale you're going to want to share at parties. **(The Frisky)** — I once asked a longtime friend why, rather than ending things with the boyfriend she lived with, she had started a complicated affair with a married man who lived nearby. She fired back, “Don’t be ridiculous—no one gets out of a relationship before securing the next one.”

That is the defining trait of “Overlappers”: they keep their current romance going until a new one is already underway. I initially disagreed. People regularly leave relationships because love has faded or anger has taken over, even when there is no backup partner waiting. But after reconsidering my friend’s history, I realized she had never done that during all the years I had known her. No matter how much she disliked her current partner, she remained with him until she had found a successor.

Her behavior baffled me. She is attractive, intelligent, and accomplished, so a brief stretch of single life was hardly likely to ruin her.

This habit is not limited to women. I have known—and, regrettably, dated—many men who rush straight from one girlfriend to the next, frequently allowing the relationships to overlap significantly, as if they were two intersecting circles in a muddy Venn diagram.

Being unattached can certainly feel frustrating or lonely, but there are several strong arguments against becoming an Overlapper—or dating one.

**1. What goes around comes around**

Overlapping is unquestionably a form of infidelity, but what distinguishes these people is that they cheat specifically to move themselves into a new relationship. Whatever label is used, an Overlapper misleads either one partner or both to achieve that goal.

Relationships founded on deception tend to create consequences later. At minimum, it will be difficult to trust someone who behaves this way. The familiar saying applies because it contains some truth: if a person cheats with you, that person may eventually cheat on you.

**2. Expect plenty of turmoil**

No breakup is pleasant, but separations triggered by unfaithfulness are usually the most volatile.

In the case of my friend and her new partner—who, surprisingly, really did leave his wife—the early stages of their romance were not filled with the affection, flowers, and excitement other new couples might enjoy. Instead, their evenings involved discussing ways to conceal assets and wondering whether their expensive attorney was ruthless enough. So much for romance.

**3. Constant demands to remain perfect**

People who cannot tolerate being alone may look self-sufficient, but they often depend on seeing an idealized version of themselves in a partner’s admiring gaze.

When that “mirror”—their significant other—develops an imperfection, such as gaining weight or losing a job, it changes how they see themselves. Because a narcissist accepts nothing short of perfection, the Overlapper then begins searching for a new mirror. In other words, anyone hoping to keep such a partner had better remain at the top of their game.

**4. It does not make an adorable origin story**

Saying, “I met my boyfriend after his puppy urinated on my foot,” makes for a classic charming first-meeting story. It includes coincidence, comedy, and—most importantly—a lovable puppy.

By contrast, “I met my boyfriend while working as his children’s nanny, and his wife gave me this black eye after discovering our affair,” is not the sort of story most people will want to repeat at social gatherings.

## The Problem With “Overlappers”

Some people never seem to be single. Before one relationship has officially ended, they are already flirting with, confiding in, or quietly dating someone new. These people can be called “Overlappers”: rather than ending one romance, taking time to recover, and eventually beginning another, they allow the two relationships to overlap.

At first, this behavior may seem understandable. Ending a relationship can be lonely, painful, and frightening. A new romantic interest offers reassurance and excitement at exactly the moment an existing partnership feels disappointing or unstable. Instead of facing an uncertain future alone, the Overlapper creates a bridge from one relationship to the next.

But that bridge is usually built on dishonesty.

Consider the familiar story of someone who insists that a new friend is “just a friend.” Text messages become more frequent, private jokes develop, and emotional intimacy grows. Meanwhile, the current partner is told there is nothing to worry about. By the time the original relationship ends, the supposed friendship is ready to become a romance—sometimes within days.

The Overlapper may claim that no physical cheating occurred. Yet the technical definition of cheating is not the only issue. Secrecy, emotional betrayal, and deliberate deception can be just as damaging. If someone is investing romantic energy in a new person while continuing to accept the loyalty and affection of a current partner, the relationship is no longer honest.

Overlapping also changes the nature of a breakup. A difficult but manageable separation can become an explosive confrontation involving accusations, hidden messages, mutual friends, and competing versions of events. The person being left may discover that the breakup was being planned long before it was announced. Worse, they may realize that the new partner had already been waiting in the background.

This creates a particularly painful form of humiliation. The abandoned partner is not merely grieving the end of a relationship; they are questioning the entire final chapter of it. They may wonder when the deception began, which conversations were genuine, and whether every denial was a lie. Instead of receiving a clear ending, they are left reconstructing the truth from fragments.

There are several reasons people overlap relationships. Some are afraid of being alone. Some depend heavily on romantic attention for their self-esteem. Others dislike confrontation and hope that a new attachment will give them the courage to leave an unhappy situation. A few enjoy the excitement of secrecy or the sense of power that comes from being desired by more than one person.

These motives may explain the behavior, but they do not excuse it. Adults are responsible for ending relationships they no longer want. Fear, insecurity, and loneliness are real, but they are not permission to mislead another person.

There are also good reasons to be cautious about dating a known Overlapper. If someone began a relationship with you before properly ending one with somebody else, you may eventually wonder whether the same thing could happen again. The secrecy that initially made the connection feel intense can later become a source of anxiety. Every new friendship, late-night message, or unexplained absence may raise an uncomfortable question: Is another overlap beginning?

The new partner may initially feel special. They may believe they rescued the Overlapper from a loveless or unhealthy relationship. Often, however, they have heard only one side of the story. The previous partner is described as cold, unreasonable, jealous, or impossible to leave. While that account may contain some truth, it can also be a convenient way of justifying betrayal.

A relationship founded on deception carries that history into the future. Trust is difficult to build when both people know how easily boundaries were crossed. Even if the new couple stays together, they may struggle with guilt, suspicion, or resentment. The qualities that made the overlap possible—avoidance, secrecy, and emotional impulsiveness—do not disappear merely because the old relationship is over.

There is a healthier alternative. If a relationship is no longer working, end it clearly and respectfully. Accept the discomfort of being alone for a while. Grieve, reflect, and take responsibility for what happened. Only then begin something new.

Being single between relationships is not a failure. It can be an important period of recovery and self-examination. It allows a person to understand what went wrong, what they truly want, and what patterns they should avoid repeating.

Overlapping may appear to offer a painless transition, but it usually transfers the pain to everyone else—and often delays it for the Overlapper as well. It breeds dishonesty, mistrust, and dramatic breakups, while giving the next relationship a damaged foundation. If a romance must end, it is better to close that chapter honestly before beginning another.

# Don’t Be An Overlapper—And Definitely Don’t Date One

An **Overlapper** is someone who begins Relationship B before officially ending Relationship A. They don’t break up so much as change trains while both are still moving, dragging a suitcase full of unresolved feelings behind them.

Overlapper logic usually sounds like this:

> “My relationship was basically over.”

“Basically over” is not the same as over. A carton of milk that’s *basically empty* can still ruin your purse.

## Why You Shouldn’t Be An Overlapper

### 1. You’re avoiding the breakup, not avoiding the pain

Overlapping feels efficient: no lonely Sundays, no sad playlists, no eating shredded cheese over the sink while wondering whether you’ll die alone.

Unfortunately, emotional processing does not accept shortcuts. All the grief, guilt, anger, and confusion you skipped will eventually arrive—probably during brunch with your shiny new partner.

### 2. Your new romance is being built on a trapdoor

Even if the new person knew you were attached, the relationship began with secrecy, blurred boundaries, or some world-class technicalities.

“We didn’t kiss until after the breakup” is not especially reassuring when you were already texting each other 97 times a day and choosing imaginary baby names.

### 3. You never learn whether you actually like the new person

Maybe they’re your soulmate. Or maybe they’re simply the first person who asked follow-up questions after three years with someone who communicated exclusively through sighs.

Until you’re single, it’s difficult to tell the difference between true compatibility and the intoxicating experience of being noticed.

### 4. You’re turning people into emotional life rafts

Partners are people, not inflatable flotation devices stationed between relationships. If you need someone waiting in the wings before you can leave, you’re making them responsible for a decision that should be yours.

Break up because the relationship is wrong—not because a replacement has passed inspection.

## Why You Shouldn’t Date An Overlapper

### 1. Their ex is still in the room

Not literally, hopefully. But emotionally? Their ex is sitting between you, eating mozzarella sticks and influencing every conversation.

Freshly overlapped people are often still fighting, grieving, comparing, stalking Instagram, dividing furniture, or maintaining suspiciously intense “closure” talks. Congratulations: your new relationship has a ghost with texting privileges.

### 2. You’ve already seen their exit strategy

Pay attention to how someone leaves, because you may be watching the trailer for your own breakup.

If they handled dissatisfaction by cultivating a secret understudy, what happens when your relationship hits a dull patch? You may not get a conversation. You may get replaced by “a friend from work who just really understands.”

### 3. Trust becomes an unpaid second job

You’ll tell yourself your situation is different. Their old relationship was dead. You’re special. They’ve changed.

Perhaps! But you may still become a part-time detective, analyzing message timestamps and asking why “Chris from Pilates” needs to send heart emojis at midnight. Love should not require forensic certification.

### 4. You’ll always wonder whether you were chosen—or used

Did they move toward you because they genuinely wanted you? Or because you provided a convenient bridge over the frightening swamp of singledom?

No one wants to discover they were less “love of my life” and more “emotional moving walkway.”

## What To Do Instead

If you’re tempted to overlap, end your current relationship cleanly. Then spend enough time alone to remember what you like, what you need, and how to attend a social event without clinging to the nearest attractive person like a baby koala.

If you’re interested in an Overlapper, say:

> “Call me when you’re fully single and have had time to process your breakup.”

Then step away. No secret flirting. No waiting-room romance. No becoming their unpaid therapist with kissing benefits.

A person who truly wants to be with you can finish one chapter before scribbling your name into the next. And if they can’t tolerate even a brief blank page, they probably aren’t ready to write anything worth reading.

counterfactuals.output:
## The Emotional Layover: Why Some People Won’t Leave Until Their Next Relationship Is Boarding

There’s a particular kind of person who treats relationships like apartments in a competitive rental market: they won’t hand over the keys until the next place is secured, inspected, and conveniently furnished.

They may insist the relationship has been “over for months.” Fascinating—because their partner apparently didn’t receive the cancellation notice. Instead, they keep one foot in the old relationship while extending the other toward a flirtatious coworker, an ex who has recently discovered therapy, or someone from the gym whose primary qualification is consistent eye contact.

Take “Sophie,” who has spent a year telling friends that her boyfriend is emotionally unavailable. She could leave, of course—but first she needs to determine whether the charming man from marketing is truly interested or merely European. Meanwhile, “Maya” has quietly revived contact with her college ex, just in case her current relationship finally collapses under the weight of all those “we need to talk” conversations they never finish.

And then there’s “Claire,” who claims she isn’t cheating because she and her new prospect have only exchanged 4,000 messages, three intimate confessions, and one hotel recommendation. No kissing, Your Honor.

Let’s be clear: realizing you have feelings for someone else is not automatically a moral catastrophe. People are messy; attraction happens. But secretly auditioning a replacement while your current partner is still appearing in the role is, at best, cowardly—and at worst, cheating with better branding. Emotional affairs count even when everyone keeps their trousers on. If you’re hiding messages, deleting threads, or describing your partner as a “roommate” to someone you fancy, the technicalities are not going to save you.

Why do people do it? Fear of loneliness, mostly. Also fear of regret, financial instability, bruised self-esteem, and the unbearable prospect of spending a Saturday night without anyone asking what they want for dinner. A backup partner offers reassurance: *See? I’m still desirable.* Unfortunately, another human being is not a flotation device.

### Four Drawbacks to Romantic Leapfrogging

1. **You never actually process the breakup.**  
   Instead of grieving, reflecting, and figuring out why you stayed unhappy, you sprint directly into a new relationship carrying the same emotional luggage—now with extra shoes.

2. **Trust starts on shaky ground.**  
   If the new romance began with secret texts and strategic omissions, both parties know what the other is capable of. Nothing says “healthy foundation” like wondering whether you’ll eventually be replaced by someone from Pilates.

3. **You turn people into insurance policies.**  
   The current partner becomes temporary housing; the prospective partner becomes an exit strategy. Neither gets treated like a full human being, which is generally frowned upon outside corporate restructuring.

4. **You avoid learning that being alone is survivable.**  
   Solitude is not a medical emergency. In fact, it can help you rediscover your standards, friendships, and ability to assemble flat-pack furniture without interpreting it as a metaphor for abandonment.

The grown-up option is painfully unglamorous: end the relationship because it needs to end, not because another person is waiting in the wings with flattering texts and excellent hair. Then spend enough time single to distinguish genuine compatibility from the intoxicating relief of being wanted.

Leave because you’re done. Not because your replacement relationship has cleared its background check.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
# The Overlapper: When One Relationship Is the Runway for the Next

An **“Overlapper”** is someone who starts a new romantic relationship before properly ending—or emotionally untangling from—the current one.

Sometimes the overlap is obvious: secret dates, suspiciously cheerful texting, and a “friend from work” who somehow knows their coffee order and childhood trauma. Other times it’s emotional: the Overlapper has mentally checked out of Relationship A while quietly auditioning candidates for Relationship B.

Think of it as relationship monkey-barring: they refuse to let go of one branch until they have a firm grip on the next.

To be clear, this isn’t the same as consensual non-monogamy, where everyone knows the arrangement. Overlapping usually involves secrecy, blurred boundaries, or using a new person as an escape hatch.

Here are four reasons it’s usually a spectacularly bad idea.

## 1. You Skip the Emotional Autopsy

After a breakup, it helps to ask uncomfortable questions: What went wrong? What did I tolerate? What did I contribute? Why did I keep dating someone who communicated exclusively through sighing?

Overlap, and you can avoid all that. The dopamine rush of the new relationship smothers the grief from the old one—temporarily.

Consider the classic story: Jamie leaves a five-year relationship and immediately moves in with Alex, the “totally platonic” climbing partner. Three months later, Alex discovers that Jamie still cries whenever the ex’s favorite song plays at the supermarket.

The feelings didn’t disappear. They just climbed into the luggage.

## 2. The New Person Becomes a Life Raft

A relationship works better when it’s a choice, not an emergency evacuation vehicle.

Overlappers often use the new partner to supply courage, housing, validation, or proof that they’re still desirable. That creates a lopsided foundation: one person thinks they’re beginning a romance; the other is fleeing a burning building while clutching a toothbrush.

Once the smoke clears, the Overlapper may realize they chose the nearest exit—not the right person.

## 3. Trust Starts With a Very Awkward Question

If someone began dating you while still attached to someone else, a tiny question may eventually appear:

**“Could they do the same thing to me?”**

It’s hard to build security when the origin story requires selective editing. Even if the new relationship becomes serious, secrecy and half-truths can linger like glitter after a party: surprisingly difficult to remove and somehow visible everywhere.

One woman joked that her boyfriend’s romantic timeline had “more creative accounting than a bankrupt theme park.” Funny—but not especially calming.

## 4. You Repeat the Pattern Instead of Fixing It

Without time alone, people often carry the same habits into the next relationship: conflict avoidance, poor boundaries, fear of abandonment, chronic attraction to emotionally unavailable musicians named Luca.

The cast changes, but the plot doesn’t.

An Overlapper may blame every ex for being “too needy,” only to discover that disappearing during difficult conversations reliably makes partners want reassurance. Who knew?

Time between relationships isn’t a punishment. It’s where you notice patterns, relearn your own preferences, and discover whether you actually enjoy pottery—or merely dated three ceramicists.

## The Bottom Line

Overlapping can feel efficient: no lonely weekends, no sad playlists, no awkward return to the apps. But relationships aren’t connecting flights. If you sprint from one to the next without collecting your emotional baggage, the baggage still arrives—usually at the worst possible moment.

End one relationship honestly. Grieve it. Learn from it. Spend enough time alone to know whether you miss your ex or merely miss having someone nearby to open stubborn jars.

Then start something new because you genuinely want that person—not because you needed somewhere soft to land.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
“Nobody leaves a relationship without having someone else lined up,” my friend said, defending her affair with the confidence of a woman explaining gravity.

This was convenient, because she had already lined up someone else: a married man who communicated primarily through disappearing messages and panic.

Her theory was simple. People don’t jump from one relationship until they’ve secured the next, like emotionally exhausted trapeze artists. According to her, overlapping isn’t betrayal; it’s logistics. Why risk being alone when you can use one person as a bridge to another?

The problem is that people are not bridges. They are more like airport terminals: complicated, overcrowded, full of baggage, and capable of shutting down completely when you behave suspiciously.

Serial relationship overlapping feels efficient because it eliminates the dreaded gap between partners—the quiet stretch where you might have to eat dinner alone, choose a Netflix show without negotiation, or confront the horrifying possibility that your personality has become 70 percent couple habits. But avoiding that gap doesn’t prevent pain. It merely forwards it to a new address.

And it usually arrives with extra postage.

The new relationship begins under the glow of escape. Your lover seems thrilling because they are not your current partner. They listen. They understand. They have never once loaded the dishwasher “wrong.” They haven’t had enough time to become ordinary, which is the unfair standard against which the existing partner is judged.

Then the breakup drama begins.

There are deleted texts, revised timelines, mutual friends forced into amateur espionage, and one person insisting, “Nothing happened until after we broke up,” with the courtroom precision of someone who has spent three weeks defining “happened.” Everyone becomes a forensic analyst. A heart emoji from February is entered into evidence. An old vacation photo acquires the emotional weight of the Zapruder film.

The overlapper often claims the old relationship was “already over,” which is a fascinating phrase because the other person is frequently still living in it.

Then comes karma—not necessarily the mystical kind, where the universe keeps a glittery ledger and sends a pigeon to ruin your coat. Social karma is enough. If you begin a relationship by demonstrating that you handle dissatisfaction through secrecy and replacement, your new partner has received a very clear product demonstration.

Every delayed reply becomes suspicious. Every work friendship develops a plot. Every “I’m going to bed early” sounds like the opening line of a documentary.

After all, your new partner knows you’re capable of maintaining two emotional realities at once. They may find this sexy during the affair, when they are the exciting secret. It becomes less charming when they are promoted to Official Partner and the position of Exciting Secret becomes vacant.

This is where insecurity moves in and starts rearranging the furniture.

The overlapper is insecure because they never proved they could survive alone. The new partner is insecure because they know how the audition process works. The ex is insecure because they’ve been retroactively informed that months of their life were apparently a waiting room.

Nobody wins, except perhaps the couples therapist who will eventually need to untangle why “working late” now causes heart palpitations.

And then there is the origin story.

Healthy couples get to say, “We met at a friend’s birthday,” or “We reached for the same bruised avocado.” Overlapping couples often have to perform verbal tax evasion.

“We met through work.”

Technically true.

“We were both going through difficult transitions.”

Also true, if “difficult transitions” means one spouse was still ordering matching Christmas pajamas.

“We were friends first.”

Yes. Friends who communicated exclusively after midnight and needed to hide their friendship behind a calculator app.

The origin story becomes an embarrassing family heirloom. It must be polished, shortened, and kept away from anyone who knows the dates. At anniversaries, the couple celebrates a beginning that cannot be clearly identified without implicating at least one of them.

“How long have you two been together?”

A pause.

A glance.

An accountant is summoned.

Of course, not every relationship that begins in overlap is doomed. Human beings are messy, relationships decay unevenly, and sometimes love appears at an inconvenient moment. But “messy things happen” is not the same as “nobody leaves without someone else lined up.” Plenty of people leave because the relationship is wrong, endure the empty space, and resist converting the next available person into emotional carry-on luggage.

That empty space matters. It teaches you whether you miss your ex or merely miss being chosen. It reveals which parts of your identity were surrendered for convenience. It gives you time to become a person again instead of a vacancy urgently seeking an applicant.

Leaving without a replacement is frightening because it requires faith that loneliness is survivable. Overlapping offers an anesthetic. But anesthetic is not healing, and a soft landing is not the same as an honest one.

My friend wanted me to believe everybody does it because universality would make it innocent. If no one leaves without another partner waiting, then betrayal becomes biology. Secrecy becomes strategy. Cowardice gets rebranded as human nature.

But sometimes the most adult thing you can do is leave with no one waiting.

No backup. No secret chat. No romantic flotation device wearing expensive cologne.

Just your suitcase, your grief, your dignity, and the mildly terrifying realization that the next person you need to be in a relationship with is yourself.

At least that origin story won’t require a fake timeline.
